FOREWORD This Indian Sta ndard ( Part 1 ) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized bv the Illumination Engineering and Luminaires Sectional Committee had been approved by the Eleetrotechnical Division Council. The object of this standard is to recommend the adoption of the test procedures that will give acceptable results in determining and reporting the photometric characteristics of luminaires. This standard ( Part 1 ) is one of the series of IndianEStandards which deals with photometry of luminaires. The series consists of the following parts: Method of photometry Part 1 Luminaires Part 2 Luminaires Part 3 Luminaires of luminaires for use in interior lighting; for road and street lighting; and for floodlighting. the methods of

In the formulation of this standard, assistance has been derived from CIE Publication No. 24 ( TC 2.4) 1973 on photometry of indoor type luminaires with tubular fluorcescent lamps issued by the International Electrotechnical Commission. This standard, when published, will supersede IS 7678 : 1975 `Method of photometric testing of incandescent type luminaires for general lighting service' which covers the method for photometric testing of filament type general lighting luminaires.

1 SCOPE 1.1 This standard covers methods of photometry for luminaires designed primarily for indoor use with lamps specified in Annex A for general lighting service and suitable for ac eIectricity supply up to 250 V at 50 Hz. 1.2 The requirements described in these recommendations relate to the following photometric characteristics:

The accuracy of photometric measurement is in turn dependent upon the apparatus used, and also on the testing procedure adopted. 4.1 Accuracy of Photometric Measurement OF TEST APPARATUS AND METHODS

The aim of these recommendations is to provide guidance for industrial laboratories to achieve a sufficient order of accuracy in photometric measurements. 4.2 Sources of Error Photometric results of a sufficient order of accuracy can only be achieved by meticulous attention to detail. In general, two kinds of error impair accuracy, namely, systematic errors, inherent in the test methods used or caused by imperfections of instruments, and

The movement of air around the bare lamp or luminaire under test will reduce the operating temperature of the lamp or lamps, thereby altering their light output. Such movement of air may be caused by draughts, air conditioning or motion of the luminaire on the photometer. The photocell should be screened so that it `sees' only the luminaire. It should be noted that many black paints have a reflection factor as high as 4 percent when new and unmarked. For angles of incidence close to the plane of such surfaces the reflection factor is much higher, where possible therefore, screening should be arranged so that a stray light from the luminaire reaches the photocell only after two or more reflections from blackend surfaces. Where only one surface can be provided it may be necessary to cover it with black velvet, black carpet, etc. The position of the mirror in relation to the luminaire is important as this error will usually increase when:

Possibly the best method of locating sources of stray light is to view by eye from the position of the photocell as the luminaire is rotated on the photometer.

The photocell and its measuring circuit should be stable in operation and not subject to fatigue maximum level of when exposed to the illuminance encountered. The combination of photocell and measuring circuit should possess essentially linear response to light up to the maximum level of illuminance encountered. Alternatively, individual readings should be corrected for non-linearity. The spectral sensitivity of the photocell should CIE spectral closely follow the standard luminous efficiency V ( h ) curve. It is recommended that the stability of the spectral response be checked periodically. A method of checking with colour filters is given in Annex E. 6.1.2 ,Measurement of Photocell Output of the photocell should be The output measured to an accuracy of &l percent. If automatic recording equipment is used for the measurement of photo current it is important that the maximum inherent errors of the equipment are determined, for example, delayed response to change in photo current, and lack of response ( a finite `dead zone' ) to small changes. 6.1.3 Additional Requirements

The constructions must provide an accurate measurement of photocell position usualIy expressed as angle to nadir together with the angle in azimuth. The measured position of photocell shall be correct to within f 0.5".

The photocell must be sensitive only to light which falls on the surface of the cell within an angle a to the normal of the cell. The angle GC should not be greater than 2.5". The cell must be of a size which permits it to view effectively the whole of the luminaire. Thus the diameter of the cell must be at least 30 mm in diameter. 6.2 Requirements for Distribution Photometers 6.2.1 Selection and Performance The selection of a distribution photometer for use in an industrial laboratory involves the aspects of acceptable accuracy as discussed in 4 and of the laboratory space available. 7.1.2 Ageing of Lamps All test lamps should be aged by cyclic operation over a period of not less than 100 hours at rated supply volts, with ballasts complying with reIevant Indian Standard, until the light output and electrical characteristics are shown by successive readings to be stable. A suggested cycle consists of a 15-minute `off period every 4 hours. Alternatively, the procedure for ageing, especially when testing Iuminaires designed for operation with high internal temperatures, may comprise 100 hours at 110 percent rated supply volts, followed by a period of 6 hours at 80�C at rated voltage. 7.1.3 Stability of Lamps Lamps should be regarded as stable when the variation between 3 successive readings in accordance with 6.1.4 below, at intervals of 15 minutes, does not exceed 1 percent. The lamp should then be switched off, cooled and switched on again and a further reading taken which should not vary by more than 1 percent. 7.1.4 Tests for

reflectance factor

By setting the photometer so that the effective position of the photocell is at nadir and moving a light source in a horizontal plane through the optical centre of the photometer, variations and in the reflectance factor of the mirror over the area transversed can be measured. The light source should have an essentially uniform light distribution in directions near the vertical and the apparent area should be approximately 0.002 8 ma ( that is, a 100 W opalescent incandescent lamp ) and the photocell placed in its normal position. The variation of the angle of incidence on the photocell and of the distance between the photoctll and the light source, when moving this, must be taken into account. 7 PREPARATION OF LAMP LUMINAIRES FOR TESTS 7.0 General The preparation of lamps and luminaires for following testing should comply with the recommendations. 7.1 Test Lamps 7.1.1 Selection of Lamps for Test for test should comply with the relevant Indian Standards ( see Annex A ) following where applicable, and with the requirements:

8.2 Calibration of Photometer Calibration of a distribution photometer or integrating sphere should be carried out with bare lamps just prior to or immediately after measurements on the luminaire. Each lamp should be photometered separately when operated from its respective ballast. The luminous flux of a lamp operated in some multi-lamp circuits is affected by the operating temperature of the other lamp ( or lamps ) in the same circuit. In such cases the other lamps not under test should remain energized but should be freely suspended horizontally outside the luminaire, in still air at 25�C.

ANNEX

E

( Clause 6.1.1 )
METHOD OF CHECKING SfABILITY OF SPECTRAL RESPONSE PHOTO-ELECTRIC CELL USING COLOUR FlLTERS OF A

It is recommended that the stability of the spectral response of a photocell and associated filter be checked periodically. This can be done simply by using the cell to make periodic measurements of the luminous transmittances of three stable colour filters. Measurements should be made at a normal High illuminance of the illuminance level. It is photocell should always be avoided. recommended that in the case of selenium photovoltaic cells, the illuminance should not exceed a level at which the cell begins to show non-linearity. In practice this is commonly in the region of 200 lux for a cell operating with zero external resistance.

Periodic measurements should be made under identical test canditions to minimise errors due to extraneous effects. The light source should be an incandescent lamp operated at the same colour temperature on each occasion, usually 2856 K. ( C.I.E. Illuminant A. )
NOTE - Filters with characteristics similar to the following are satisfactory for this measurement: Blue Filter Green Filter Red Filter

: Corning

Type CS l-62, Glass Type 5 900 or Schott Type BG 28/l mm.

: Corning : Corning

Type CS 4-64, Glass Type 4 010 or Schott Type VG 6/l mm.

Standard Mark The use of the Standard Mark is governed by the provisions of the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 and the Rules and Regulations made thereunder. The Standard Mark on products covered by an Indian Standard conveys the assurance that they have been produced to comply with the requirements of that standard under a well defined system of inspection, testing and quality control which is devised and supervised by BIS and operated by the producer. Standard marked products are also continuously checked by BIS for conformity to that standard as a further safeguard. Details of conditions under which a Iicence for the use of the Standard Mark may be granted to manufacturers or producers may be obtained from the Bureau of Indian Standards.

Bureau of Indian Standards BIS is a statutory institution established under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 to promote harmonious development of the activities of standardization, marking and quality certification of goods and attending to connected matters in the country.
